slides.title: Know Your Tools
slides.subtitle: What's available and when to reach for each.
slides.takeaway: Different tools have different strengths — pick the right one for the task.

notes.intent: Orient the audience on the tool landscape so they know what's available and when to reach for each.
notes.summary: Quick overview — don't pitch any single tool. The group is already using a mix of these. Highlight that IT has approved enterprise versions of some tools. Mention that consistency within a project matters more than constantly switching between tools.

tiles.title: ChatGPT
tiles.description: Strong at breaking down complex problems, explaining reasoning, and retaining project context across long conversations.

tiles.title: Copilot
tiles.description: Best when working inside Microsoft ecosystem apps — Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams. IT-approved enterprise version available.

tiles.title: Claude
tiles.description: Excels at nuanced analysis, long-document processing, and technical writing. Claude Code extends it into full development workflows.

tiles.title: Grok
tiles.description: Access to real-time X/Twitter posts and conversations. Useful for research on trending topics and recent public discourse.

tiles.title: NotebookLM
tiles.description: Upload documents and ask questions against them. Great for searching through manuals, specs, and technical documentation.

tiles.title: Cursor
tiles.description: AI-powered code editor. Understands your codebase and helps with scripting, debugging, and building out projects faster.

slides.title: AI as a Force Multiplier
slides.subtitle: Reframing the conversation from replacement to amplification.
slides.takeaway: AI is a power tool. The craftsperson still drives the work.

notes.intent: Address the elephant in the room — job displacement anxiety — and reframe AI as augmentation.
notes.summary: This came directly from Matthew Byrnes' feedback. Acknowledge the Amazon layoffs and broader concerns honestly, but reframe: the engineers who thrive will be the ones who leverage these tools, not the ones who ignore them or surrender their judgment to them.

content.problemDescription: How do I use AI without it replacing the skills that make me valuable?
results: Amplifies your expertise — doesn't substitute for it
The person asking the question matters more than the tool answering
Move faster and explore approaches you wouldn't have considered

slides.title: The Prompt Matters
slides.subtitle: Same question, dramatically different results.
slides.takeaway: The quality of your output is directly proportional to the quality of your input.

notes.intent: Make prompt engineering tangible with a before/after that resonates with the engineering audience.
notes.summary: Walk through both prompts live if time allows. Emphasize: role context, specificity, referencing standards, and stating what you want the output to look like. These techniques apply regardless of which AI tool you're using.

sections.label: The Prompt
items: Tell me about fire sprinkler deflectors

sections.label: What You Get
items: Generic Wikipedia-level overview
No relevance to your specific problem
Have to ask 5 follow-ups to get useful output

sections.label: The Prompt
items: Role: fire protection engineer evaluating pendent deflector
Context: EC coverage at 15-ft spacing, tine angle at 40°
Question: distribution changes if slots widen by 2mm
Standard: reference NFPA 13 criteria

sections.label: What You Get
items: Domain-specific analysis with relevant standards
Actionable engineering insight
Single-prompt result you can work with

slides.title: How These Models Actually Work
slides.subtitle: A 3-minute mental model — no math required.
slides.takeaway: These models predict — they don't understand. Knowing this changes how you interact with them.

notes.intent: Give the audience a basic mental model of how LLMs work without going too deep into the math.
notes.summary: Keep this brief — 3-5 minutes max. The key insight is that these systems are sophisticated pattern matchers, not reasoning engines. This explains why they can be confidently wrong, why prompt quality matters so much, and why your domain expertise is the critical ingredient they lack.

stages.title: TRAINING
bullets: Fed billions of text documents — books, code, technical papers
Learns statistical relationships between words and concepts
No human-like understanding, just massive pattern exposure

stages.title: PATTERN RECOGNITION
bullets: Predicts what comes next based on learned patterns
Probability distributions, not reasoning or comprehension
This is why prompt quality matters so much

stages.title: GENERATION
bullets: Produces coherent, contextual responses
Can follow instructions and work through steps
Confidence does not equal correctness

slides.title: When Not to Trust AI
slides.subtitle: Limitations you need to internalize before relying on output.
slides.takeaway: Trust but verify. AI gets you to 80% faster — your expertise handles the last 20%.

notes.intent: Build credibility by showing maturity — we're not just cheerleading for AI, we're being honest about limitations.
notes.summary: This slide lands well with skeptics. Give a concrete example of AI confidently producing a wrong answer — ideally something from your own experience. The point is not to scare people off, it's to calibrate expectations so they use these tools effectively.

columns.title: Hallucinations
items: AI can fabricate citations, statistics, and technical specs
Confident tone does not mean correct content
Always verify claims against primary sources

columns.title: Domain Blind Spots
items: Models lack Victaulic-specific institutional knowledge
NFPA/UL listing nuances require human judgment
Manufacturing constraints aren't in the training data

columns.title: Good Habits
items: Treat AI output as a first draft, not a final answer
Cross-reference critical data before acting on it
Use AI to accelerate research — then apply your expertise

slides.title: Building Context Over Time
slides.subtitle: Why consistency with one model beats tool-hopping.
slides.takeaway: Context compounds. The longer you invest in one model per project, the more it gives back.

notes.intent: Share a practical insight most people haven't considered — consistency over tool-hopping.
notes.summary: This is a practical tip that applies to everyone. Use a quick example: if you've been working with Claude on a project for two weeks, it has the full history of your decisions, your preferences, and your project structure. Starting over in ChatGPT loses all of that context. The tool you commit to matters less than the fact that you commit.

stages.title: WEEK 1
bullets: Generic responses — the model doesn't know you yet
You're providing full context every time
Feels like starting from scratch on each prompt

stages.title: WEEK 2
bullets: Model learns your patterns and preferences
References prior decisions and project structure
Less repetition, faster iteration

stages.title: WEEK 4
bullets: Anticipates what you need before you ask
Maintains full history of your project context
Switching tools now would reset all of this

content.caption: The tool you commit to matters less than the fact that you commit.
